title: Area XI review: Postflight Procedures
intro: These 20 questions cover Area XI's one taught Task, After Landing, Parking, and Securing, at the commercial level. They follow a for-hire day from the rollout and runway exit through the taxi in, parking, fueling, the postflight walkaround and write-ups, to securing the airplane for the night.

questions.q: You land a charter passenger on Runway 36 with the wind from 300 at 14 knots. As you slow on the rollout, how should you use the controls?
options: Hold the ailerons neutral, since they do nothing once the wheels are on the ground, and steer with the brakes
Hold right aileron, away from the wind, so the airplane will not weathervane
Hold left aileron, into the wind, to keep the upwind wing from rising, and keep direction with rudder and nosewheel steering
Raise the flaps right away to kill lift, then deal with the ailerons once you have stopped
questions.why: Wind from 300 on Runway 36 comes from the left, so the left wing is the upwind wing. On the after-landing roll, keep it from rising with aileron while you hold direction with rudder or nosewheel steering. As the airplane slows, the ailerons get weaker and the crosswind lifts the upwind wing more, so more aileron is needed, and at the stop the control is held fully toward the wind [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]. Neutral ailerons let the upwind wing lift, and putting off the ailerons until you stop leaves the wing unprotected during the roll. Flap changes also wait: change nothing until the whole airplane is past the hold short line [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]].

questions.q: The runway is short and you need firm braking. The nosewheel is down and you have directional control. Which technique does the AFH call for?
options: Apply the brakes firmly and smoothly, short of a skid
Pump the brakes: apply, release and reapply so the tires never skid
Lock the wheels, since a skid stops the airplane fastest
Brake hard before the nosewheel touches down to save runway
questions.why: Start braking after the nosewheel is on the ground and directional control is established, then brake firmly and smoothly as needed. Pumping the brakes does not make braking more effective, and if the tires skid, braking becomes ineffective [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

questions.q: You fly a retractable-gear airplane. On a hot day, at 40 knots on the rollout, you want to open the cowl flaps and raise the wing flaps so you are ready to taxi. The POH calls for no after-landing items during the rollout. What is best?
options: Do both now, since cowl flaps and flaps are on the after-landing checklist anyway
Open the cowl flaps now but leave the wing flaps for later, since the cowl flap control is far from the gear handle
Raise the wing flaps now, since flaps up always help braking, and leave the cowl flaps for the ramp
Finish the rollout, taxi until the whole airplane is past the hold lines, stop, then positively identify each control and run the after-landing checklist
questions.why: Unless good operating practice says otherwise, complete the landing roll and clear the runway before operating any lever or switch, which greatly reduces the chance of retracting the gear on the ground [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]. Do the after-landing checklist after a complete stop beyond the runway holding position markings. Raising the flaps on the rollout is only for when the manufacturer recommends it, such as some short-field landings, and even then you positively identify the flap handle first [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. Pilots have retracted the gear instead of the flaps while still rolling [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

questions.q: You land long on Runway 9 at a towered airport. The first turn you can make is onto Runway 4, which crosses yours. The next taxiway is 1,000 feet farther on. The tower has said nothing about where to exit. What do you do?
options: Turn onto Runway 4, since it is the first available exit
Continue to the taxiway and exit there, since you may not exit onto another runway unless ATC authorizes it
Stop on Runway 9 at the intersection and wait for the tower to tell you what to do
Turn onto Runway 4 and hold just past the edge of Runway 9
questions.why: Exit without delay at the first available taxiway or where ATC tells you, but never exit the landing runway onto another runway unless ATC authorizes it. At a towered airport, don't stop or reverse course on the runway without ATC approval, so stopping at the intersection is also wrong [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

questions.q: You clear Runway 28 at a busy towered airport, flying single pilot. The whole airplane is past the hold lines and you have stopped. In what order does AC 91-73B have you work from here?
options: Call ground first, then do the after-landing checklist while you taxi to save time
Call ground, run the checklist while you wait for a reply, and look at the airport diagram once you reach the ramp
Do the after-landing checklist, call ground, read back the instructions, review the airport diagram, then monitor your progress to parking
Taxi toward the ramp you expect to use, then call ground when you get there
questions.why: AC 91-73B lists it in that order: do the after-landing items, contact ground for taxi instructions, read them back, review the airport diagram and monitor your progress to parking. Its note says to do the after-landing items once the whole airplane is past the hold short line, before contacting ATC [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(h)]]. Taxiing on toward the ramp first is wrong: once all parts of the airplane are past the holding position markings, you must hold unless ATC gives further instructions, and a taxi clearance comes from ground [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

questions.q: Ground clears you: 'Taxi to the FBO via Alpha.' Your airport diagram shows that Alpha crosses Runway 15 on the way. Nobody said anything about Runway 15. What is correct?
options: Hold short of Runway 15 and get a clearance to cross; a taxi clearance to parking does not authorize entering or crossing any runway
Cross Runway 15, since the clearance to the FBO includes every runway on the route
Cross Runway 15 if no one is on final, since you are already in contact with ground
Ask for a Standard Taxi Route instead, since an STR includes the runway crossings
questions.why: Ground's taxi clearance to parking does not authorize the aircraft to enter or cross any runway, and if you don't know the route you should ask for specific instructions [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]. An STR doesn't help: an STR instruction does not give or imply a clearance to cross a runway [[33:263|AIM 4-3-20]].

questions.q: Taxiing in at night, ground tells you to give way to a business jet crossing ahead, and you stop. What does the AIM suggest you do with your taxi light?
options: Leave it on so the jet's pilot can see you are there
Turn it off while you are stopped or yielding, and turn it on when you move again
Turn on the landing light as well, to be more visible
Turn it off and turn on the strobes instead
questions.why: To show your intent, consider having the taxi light on when moving or about to move, and off when stopped or yielding to other ground traffic. Strobes should stay off during taxi if they would affect the vision of other pilots or ground crews [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

questions.q: On your commercial checkride you stop past the hold lines, do the after-landing items from memory in a smooth flow, then read the after-landing checklist to confirm each one. The examiner asks if that is acceptable. What is the best answer?
options: No. The AFH says every checklist must be read and done one item at a time
Yes. Once the flow is done, the checklist is optional for an experienced pilot
No. After landing is not one of the phases that calls for a checklist
Yes. A checklist need not be a do-list, as long as you really use it to confirm every item
questions.why: The AFH says checklists need not be do-lists: you may do the actions, then use the checklist to make sure they are all done, but only if you are really committed to using it. After landing, and engine shutdown and securing, are on its minimum list of checklist phases. Pilots who stop taking checklists seriously drift into relying on memory alone [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

questions.q: You park on an open transient ramp with no marshaller. The wind tonight is forecast from 270 at 15 knots. Which choice best follows the AFH?
options: Park nose west into the forecast wind, where other airplanes' prop or jet blast will not hit yours, then roll a little straight ahead to straighten the nosewheel
Park nose east, right behind a parked business jet, since the jet blocks the wind
Take any tie-down, as long as the tail faces the wind to protect the elevator
Park nose west and stop in the middle of a turn, so the cocked nosewheel holds the airplane in place
questions.why: Unless you are in a designated, supervised area, pick a spot and heading where other airplanes' prop or jet blast will not strike yours, head into the existing or forecast wind when you can, and after stopping let the airplane roll straight ahead a little to straighten the nosewheel [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Behind a jet is the worst spot: blast from powerful aircraft can make a light airplane uncontrollable [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

questions.q: After a charter leg you shut down: mixture at idle cutoff, magneto switch OFF, master OFF. A lineman reaches in to turn the propeller a few inches so a blade is clear of the tie-down rope. Which assumption does the AFH call for while anyone is touching the propeller?
options: The propeller is safe, because the magneto switch is OFF
The propeller is safe, because the master switch is OFF and the mixture is at idle cutoff
The ignition is on, because a faulty switch can read OFF and still let the magneto fire
The propeller is safe once the engine has been stopped for a minute or more
questions.why: The AFH says that while touching a propeller you should always assume the ignition is on. The magneto switch works by short-circuiting the magneto to turn the ignition off, and if the switch is faulty it can be in the OFF position and still let current flow, so the engine could start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. A switch position, the master switch, the mixture setting or a wait does not remove that risk. This is also why the shutdown includes a brief magneto check at idle [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

questions.q: At a fuel stop you have three charter passengers. You will stay at the airplane to watch the fueling. The FBO is across a busy ramp. What does the AFH advise?
options: Keep them seated in the airplane during fueling so they don't wander onto the ramp
Get them out of the airplane, and since they will not be under your direct supervision, have someone escort them to the FBO
Let them walk to the FBO on their own; your job is the fueling
Walk them over yourself and let the lineman fuel alone, since he checks the grade anyway
questions.why: During refueling, take all passengers out of the airplane and watch the fueling yourself to make sure the correct fuel and quantity go in and the caps and cowls are secured. Passengers who aren't under the pilot's direct supervision should have an escort for their safety and for ramp security [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

questions.q: You use a self-serve 100LL pump that has a grounding cable. What must happen before you remove the fuel cap?
options: Run a little fuel through the nozzle into a cup to check the color
Nothing, since static only matters when a fuel truck is used
Clip the ground wire to the pump only, since the tires ground the airplane
Attach the ground wire to the airplane
questions.why: Static builds up from fuel flowing through the hose and nozzle, not only from trucks, so attach a ground wire to the airplane before the fuel cap comes off. Then bond the nozzle to the airplane before fueling starts and keep it bonded the whole time [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]].

questions.q: At a grass strip the only fuel is in cans, and you must pour it through a chamois filter and a funnel. What does the PHAK say?
options: Pour through a plastic bucket and funnel, since plastic does not carry a static charge
Ground the airplane and bond the nozzle, chamois filter and funnel to it; never use a plastic bucket or other nonconductive container
Skip the bonding, since the chamois drains away static
Bond only the can to the funnel; the airplane itself does not need to be grounded
questions.why: Fuel passing through a chamois increases the static charge. The airplane must be grounded and the nozzle, chamois filter and funnel bonded to it. A can should be connected to the grounding post or the funnel, and a plastic bucket or other nonconductive container must never be used [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]].

questions.q: After a two-hour charter leg you find a film of oil along the belly behind the cowling. Which response matches the AFH postflight inspection?
options: Look near and around the cowling for oil streaks and around the oil breather for too much oil discharge, bring the oil to the POH level, and write up what you found
Wipe it off, since a little belly oil is normal, and say nothing
Check the brakes, since oil on the belly usually comes from a brake leak
Top the oil off and leave the cause for the next pilot's preflight
questions.why: The AFH postflight inspection has you check near and around the cowling for oil or fuel streaks and around the oil breather for excessive oil discharge, then bring the oil to AFM/POH levels [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Documenting the discrepancy is part of the Task (ACS CA.XI.A.S4), and the entry goes in the maintenance or discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

questions.q: Your charter operator's airplane has an FAA-approved MEL and Letter of Authorization. On the postflight you find a position light inoperative, and tomorrow's flight is in daylight. What is correct?
options: Defer it under 14 CFR 91.213(d) instead, since that is simpler and either method works
No entry is needed for a daylight flight; just leave the switch off
Enter it in the maintenance or discrepancy record, then have it repaired or deferred under the MEL's terms and procedures
It must be repaired before any flight, since position lights can never be deferred
questions.why: Once an operator has an MEL and an LOA, using the MEL is mandatory for that airplane, and all deferrals follow its terms and procedures. With an MEL, a pilot who finds position lights inoperative before a daytime flight makes an entry in the maintenance or discrepancy record, and the item is then repaired or deferred under the MEL [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. So 91.213(d) is not an option here.

questions.q: No MEL. On the postflight you find the cabin dome light dead. It is not on any required list, no AD covers it, and tomorrow's flight is day VFR. You pull its circuit breaker and placard it 'Inoperative'. Who may decide that it is not a hazard to the airplane?
options: Only a mechanic who holds an inspection authorization
A pilot certificated and appropriately rated under part 61, or a person certificated and appropriately rated to maintain the airplane
Anyone, including a non-pilot passenger, because it is only a dome light
Only the FSDO, by issuing a special flight permit
questions.why: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d)(4), the determination is made by a certificated, appropriately rated pilot or by a person certificated and appropriately rated to maintain the aircraft [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. A special flight permit under 91.213(e) is the way to move an airplane whose inoperative item cannot be deferred.

questions.q: You fly paid sightseeing tours for a part 91 operator with no approved inspection program. After today's last flight the airplane shows 2,487.6 hours time in service. Its last annual or 100-hour inspection was at 2,391.0 hours. Tomorrow two paid tours of 2.0 hours each are booked. What is correct?
options: Fly both, since 91.409(b) allows up to 10 extra hours
Fly neither, since the inspection is due once fewer than 5 hours remain
Fly both, as long as the extra hours are counted against the next 100-hour interval
Fly the first tour only; 3.4 hours remain, so the inspection must be done before the second paid tour
questions.why: Hours used: 2,487.6 minus 2,391.0 = 96.6. Hours left: 100 minus 96.6 = 3.4. One 2.0-hour tour leaves 1.4 hours, and the second 2.0-hour tour would carry paying passengers past 100 hours. Carrying persons for hire needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. The 10-hour allowance is only for flying en route to a place where the inspection can be done, not for more paid tours, and the rule has no 5-hour trigger [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

questions.q: You fly a part 135 charter. In cruise on the last leg, the number 2 com radio went silent for about ten minutes, then worked again by itself. Another pilot flies the airplane in the morning. What does 14 CFR 135.65(b) require?
options: Nothing, since the radio works now and a fault that clears itself is not an irregularity
Tell the next pilot in person, and make an entry only if it happens again
Make an entry only if you diverted or landed early because of it
Enter it in the aircraft maintenance log, because the rule covers each mechanical irregularity that comes to your attention during flight time
questions.why: The PIC must enter, or have entered, in the aircraft maintenance log each mechanical irregularity that comes to the pilot's attention during flight time. Before each flight the PIC must find out the status of each irregularity entered at the end of the preceding flight, which only works if the entry exists [[6:21|14 CFR 135.65(b)]]. The rule does not limit entries to faults that persist, repeat or cause a diversion. Whoever then corrects or defers the item records that action in the same log [[6:21|14 CFR 135.65(c)]].

questions.q: After securing your airplane late at night, you see someone trying the doors of parked airplanes on the GA ramp. Which number does the AIM give for reporting suspicious activity to the TSA?
options: Flight service, on 122.2 MHz
The emergency frequency, 121.5 MHz
AOPA's Airport Watch Program, 866-427-3287
The local FSDO's main phone line
questions.why: The AIM says to report suspicious activity to the TSA by calling AOPA's Airport Watch Program, 866-427-3287 [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]]. That is part of airport security procedures (ACS CA.XI.A.R3).

questions.q: It is the end of a long, six-leg charter day. Taxiing in, you notice the ammeter flickering, and you find yourself staring at it. What does the PHAK warn about this kind of moment?
options: Nothing, since the risky part of the flight is over once you land
Fatigue, stress and work overload can make you fixate on one item and lose your overall situational awareness
Fatigue makes pilots more alert to small problems, so this is a good sign
Fixation is only a problem when flying by instruments
questions.why: Fatigue, stress and work overload can make a pilot fixate on a single item and lose overall situational awareness, and many accidents start with a distraction that began as a minor problem, such as a gauge that is not reading correctly [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Distraction and fixation crowd out more important tasks [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Application: keep your eyes outside, stop clear of traffic, then look into it and write it up.
